description:
Project Vision:
We aim to solve the "Flame in Freefall" challenge by leveraging AI, Computer Vision, and ML models to analyze NASA’s microgravity combustion data. Our goal is to predict flame behavior and enhance fire safety in space missions.
​Looking for Team Members:
​AI/ML & Data Analysis
​UI/UX & Web Development
​Content Writing & Pitching
summary: LUMEN is a browser screen for one question: how a droplet flame ended on the International Space Station. DIU Smart X built it for the 2026 challenge Flame in Freefall. Cabin air is a design choice. Oxygen, nitrogen, helium, the carbon monoxide column, pressure, and droplet size all change that ending. LUMEN uses only NASA PSI-69, the FLEX table from the Physical Sciences Informatics repository: 261 usable burns out of 274. A gradient-boosted model, trained with scikit-learn and run in the browser, predicts extinction, disruption, or completion. It names the five nearest recorded tests and shows that test's recorded burn time. Held-out accuracy is 75 percent. Always guessing extinction scores 69 percent. Outside the recorded range, or in lunar or Mars gravity, the score is withheld. LUMEN does not say whether a fire will start, and it does not detect or extinguish a cabin fire. The code is public at https://github.com/Uzzal-169/LUMEN
details:
LUMEN screens a proposed cabin atmosphere against droplet burns NASA already flew on the station. The user sets oxygen, nitrogen, helium, the carbon monoxide column, pressure, droplet size, and fuel. A gradient-boosted classifier running in the browser predicts extinction, disruption, or completion. The page then lists the five nearest PSI-69 rows and the recorded burn time of the nearest test. That time is how long that droplet burned. It is not a forecast of a cabin fire.

On the Station preset, the nearest row is 20CAL08: methanol, oxygen 0.21, about 1 atmosphere, recorded disruption, burn time 4.3 seconds. Dropping oxygen to 0.20 moves the same model to extinction. Moon, Mars, and rover air withhold the score, because those gravities are outside the FLEX flights. The screen says it is not guessing.

Held-out accuracy is 75 percent. Always guessing extinction scores 69 percent. Recall is about 88 percent for extinction, 60 percent for disruption, and 22 percent for completion. Completion has only 27 rows.

Who it helps: a habitat planner comparing a mix before flight, and a judge or student who needs the recorded burn named beside the score. It does not watch a cabin, detect smoke, or put a fire out.

Tools: TypeScript, React, and Vite in the browser; Python and scikit-learn for the fit; the trained model exported to JSON so the demo runs offline. The Ask panel may phrase an answer with Azure OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini. The number always comes from the local model and the PSI-69 table. With no network, a fixed template answers from the same numbers.

Super intelligence was used to draft code, this page text, and the English narration. The 30-second video voice is Microsoft neural speech, en-US-JennyNeural, generated with edge-tts. The flame on screen is a capture of the app, not a generated picture. The team chose the data limit, checked every quoted figure, and rejected any score the table does not support.
